summary: Designed the platform for the full T-1 scope (7 features, 21 stories) against all three approved upstream disciplines: one single compute host (Nginx + C-API + colocated C-SQL/C-VEC on an encrypted data volume), with C-NLU (Bedrock) and a managed secrets store the only off-host dependencies. Resolved security_nfr's Open Item OI-11 (PLA-2: Chroma runs embedded/persistent-local, not networked, keeping TB-4 the same-process boundary security_nfr already analysed and leaving their conditional mTLS rejection undisturbed). Carried out SEC-9 (data-at-rest/file-permission boundary, explicitly recorded upstream as platform's requirement, not security_nfr's to implement) as PLA-4: dedicated non-root OS user, encrypted volume, no other principal with read access. Sized compute (~2 vCPU/2 GiB) with stated evidence (NFR-9's single-instance/no-HA scope, NLU compute offloaded to Bedrock per SOL-3/TB-5, NFR-3's two-session concurrency target) rather than a bare number, tagged [INFERRED -- needs confirmation] and carried to Open Item OI-14. Defined 3 environments (dev/ci/demo) and a promotion flow requiring ci to pass plus an explicit human-triggered deploy with a pre-deploy backup (PLA-7), rollback mechanisms for code-only, schema-affecting, and host-failure cases, and an operational signal design (process supervision + host metrics/logs + alarms, PLA-8) with no APM platform introduced (matches the explicit 'modest, not enterprise-scale' sizing instruction given constraints.budget_usd is null). Recorded 9 decisions (PLA-1..PLA-9), including PLA-9 which places SEC-11's rate limiting at the reverse-proxy layer as a defense-in-depth interim measure without duplicating or resolving security_nfr's already-recorded, still-open returned_findings entry (RF-1/V-SEC2, owned by data_integration) -- deliberately not re-raised here per this task's own instruction not to duplicate it. Traced all 21 stories to platform-specific verification_scenarios (persistence-across-redeploy, IAM/secrets scoping, latency/sizing confirmation, rollback-safety), with operation_ids/entity_names recorded as [] and not_applicable per the same disclosed check-artifacts narrowed-tool-scope workaround solution and security_nfr already used. Independently recomputed all 8 upstream source hashes (3 from Workflow 1, 5 from this workflow's own already-approved disciplines); all 8 matched exactly -- no new drift found. Recorded 4 new open items (OI-14..OI-17), none blocking.

decisions.choice: One single compute host runs Nginx (TLS termination, static C-WEB hosting, reverse proxy), C-API, and both data stores' on-disk state (C-SQL's SQLite file, C-VEC's embedded Chroma persistent directory) colocated on the same encrypted data volume. C-NLU (Bedrock) remains genuinely off-host, unchanged from solution's TB-5 boundary.
alternatives: A multi-service container-orchestration platform (ECS/Kubernetes) with C-API, C-VEC, and static hosting as separate services
Separate static hosting via S3+CloudFront for C-WEB
decisions.rationale: solution's SOL-1 already fixed a single modular-monolith backend; security_nfr's NFR-9 explicitly scopes to single-instance, best-effort availability with no HA target. Colocating C-SQL/C-VEC's files with C-API keeps TB-3/TB-4 as the same-process trust zone security_nfr already analysed -- introducing a network hop here would silently invalidate that analysis and reopen security_nfr's own conditionally-rejected mTLS control.
decisions.source: solution SOL-1, SOL-7; security_nfr NFR-9, Section 2.2 (TB-3/TB-4), Section 4.2 (HA rejection)

decisions.choice: Chroma (C-VEC) runs in embedded/persistent-local mode -- an in-process library instance inside C-API writing to a persistent directory on the same host -- not as a separate, networked Chroma server process. Resolves security_nfr's Open Item OI-11.
alternatives: A standalone, networked Chroma server C-API talks to over the network
decisions.rationale: solution's SOL-9 explicitly left this deployment-mode choice to platform; security_nfr's Open Item OI-11 names exactly this decision as changing TB-4's threat profile depending on which way it goes. Choosing embedded means TB-4 remains the same-process/same-host boundary security_nfr already analysed -- no revisit of that analysis or the conditionally-rejected mTLS control is triggered.
decisions.source: solution SOL-9; security_nfr Open Item OI-11, Section 2.2 (TB-4), Section 4.2 (mTLS rejection)

decisions.choice: One instance in the ~2 vCPU / 2 GiB RAM class (e.g. AWS t3.small-class or nearest equivalent).
decisions.rationale: NFR-9 caps ambition at single-instance/best-effort; the compute-heavy work (model inference, embedding generation) happens inside Bedrock, off this host, per SOL-3/TB-5; NFR-3's concurrency target is two sessions, not a production population. [INFERRED -- needs confirmation] since no target repository exists to profile against -- see Open Item OI-14.
decisions.source: security_nfr NFR-3, NFR-6, NFR-7, NFR-9; solution SOL-3

decisions.choice: C-SQL's file and C-VEC's persistent directory live on a dedicated, encrypted data volume; both are owned by a dedicated, non-root OS user the C-API process runs as; containing directories are permissioned so no other OS principal on the host has read access.
alternatives: Default root-owned or world-readable application directories
decisions.rationale: security_nfr's SEC-9 is explicitly recorded as 'a requirement on platform, not implemented by this discipline' -- this decision is platform's own carrying-out of that requirement, not a re-derivation of why it is needed.

decisions.choice: The Bedrock-invocation IAM credential (SEC-6) is delivered via the host's own IAM instance profile/role, never a long-lived access key on disk. The shared-login credential's hashed secret and the session-signing key (SEC-1/SEC-3) are stored in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store (SecureString) and injected as environment variables at process start.
alternatives: A long-lived IAM user access key stored on the host
decisions.rationale: Directly carries out SEC-3 (credential storage) and SEC-6 (least-privilege Bedrock egress) with a concrete, named AWS mechanism, rather than leaving 'how' open.

decisions.choice: Three environments -- dev (local/individual, may stub Bedrock), ci (ephemeral, per-commit, mocked externals, no real spend), demo (the one long-lived deployed environment, real credentials, real Bedrock calls).
alternatives: A single environment with no automated ci gate
decisions.rationale: Matches the 'small demo, not enterprise scale' framing while still giving every change an automated gate before it can reach demo.

decisions.choice: ci must pass before a build is deployable; promoting a build to demo is always an explicit, human-triggered step, never automatic; that step always takes a timestamped backup of demo's SQLite file and Chroma persistent directory immediately before proceeding.
decisions.rationale: Ties the release process directly to root CLAUDE.md's own standing rule on destructive/risky operations, and gives the rollback mechanism something real to restore from.
decisions.source: Root CLAUDE.md ('never run a destructive operation... without an explicit human confirmation step first'); security_nfr NFR-3 / data_integration DAT-3

decisions.choice: Process-level auto-restart, plus CloudWatch-class host metrics and SEC-10-compliant application-log shipping, alarmed on restart count, 5xx rate, disk-space threshold, and Bedrock error rate. No distributed-tracing/APM platform is introduced.
alternatives: No centralized log/metric shipping (manual log inspection only)
decisions.rationale: The cheapest AWS-native option that still gives a genuine 'did it go wrong' signal, matching the modest-not-enterprise sizing instruction given constraints.budget_usd is null.

decisions.choice: The reverse proxy (Nginx) in front of C-API can enforce a request-rate ceiling (e.g. limit_req, keyed by session cookie or client IP) as an infrastructure-layer placement for SEC-11's per-session rate limit, usable as soon as Workflow 3/4 build the application, independent of whether data_integration's API contract has yet added the formal 429 response schema.
alternatives: Waiting until the app-level 429 response exists before adding any rate limiting at all
Building the actual application-level throttling/response logic in this discipline's own artifact
decisions.rationale: Gives a real, deployable control today without overstepping into the contract change that is legitimately data_integration's to make. Does not resolve, duplicate, or supersede security_nfr's already-recorded returned_findings entry RF-1/V-SEC2 -- only names where platform's own layer can help meanwhile.
decisions.source: security_nfr SEC-11, Open Item OI-13, returned_findings[0] (RF-1, acknowledged, not resolved by this discipline)

open_items.detail: data_integration has not yet defined a schema-migration/versioning mechanism for C-SQL (e.g. Alembic or an equivalent). Platform's backup-before-deploy/restore-on-rollback procedure (PLA-7) is the only safety net for a schema-affecting deploy until one exists, and does not by itself support running two schema versions side by side during a gradual migration.
open_items.source: PLA-7; Section 6.2 of this discipline's document
open_items.resolution_needed: Before a second schema change ships, adopt an explicit migration-versioning tool; until then, every schema-affecting deploy must go through PLA-7's backup step.

open_items.resolution_needed: Confirm the target AWS account, region, and approved Bedrock model ARN(s) before Workflow 4 provisions real infrastructure.

open_items.detail: No application-level health-check endpoint exists in data_integration's approved API contract. Platform's monitoring (PLA-8) currently relies on process/port-level liveness only, which cannot distinguish 'the process is up' from 'the process is up but stuck' (e.g. a held SQLite lock).
open_items.source: PLA-8; Section 6.3 of this discipline's document
open_items.resolution_needed: Consider a lightweight /health endpoint in a future API-contract revision; until then, platform's signal remains process/port-level only.

validation.summary: platform v1.0 is a strong, well-boundaried draft: PLA-2 genuinely resolves security_nfr's Open Item OI-11 (embedded-vs-networked Chroma) rather than restating the question -- it picks embedded mode and explicitly confirms TB-4 stays the same-process boundary security_nfr already analysed, so no mTLS revisit is triggered. PLA-4 genuinely carries out SEC-9's data-at-rest/file-permission requirement (dedicated non-root OS user, encrypted volume, no other OS principal with read access) -- a real implementation, not something adjacent. PLA-9's reverse-proxy-layer rate limiting is correctly scoped as an interim, additive control: it does not mark security_nfr's returned_findings entry RF-1/V-SEC2 resolved, does not claim to have added the missing login/logout/429 API surface, and does not introduce any new open item that restates RF-1/OI-13 (platform's own OI-14..OI-17 are all genuinely distinct, forward-looking items). All 21 traceability rows' acceptance_criteria were spot-checked against workflow-1's roles/stories.json and matched verbatim (US-1, US-9, US-13, US-16, US-21 checked in full); operation_ids/entity_names are correctly recorded as [] with a not_applicable note matching the same disclosed check-artifacts narrowed-tool-scope workaround solution and security_nfr already used -- not a new or inconsistent pattern. NFR-1 through NFR-10 (read directly from security_nfr's own Section 5 table, not just platform's paraphrase) are each either addressed with a stated mechanism or explicitly out of platform's carrying scope for a stated reason; none is silently unmet. No document/state drift was found between platform.json and the published PLATFORM-DESIGN document (unlike the drift pattern caught in two of the three prior discipline reviews) -- open items, checks, and self-verification bullets all agree word-for-word between the two. No script/IaC/config is included; the design/Workflow-4-implementation boundary is stated explicitly and never crossed. No placeholders, no credential-like strings, no real-looking PII found (pattern check only). One low-severity finding below: I have no hashing/Bash tool in this session and could not independently recompute any of the 8 claimed SHA-256 values from actual file bytes, so platform's own checks[] claim of an independent sha256sum computation is corroborated only by cross-file string consistency, not verified at the byte level.
validation.independence: Read platform.json, the full published PLATFORM-DESIGN document, and workflow.json directly. Cross-read solution.json + SOLUTION-ARCHITECTURE document, data_integration.json + all 3 of its artifacts, security_nfr.json + the full SECURITY-AND-NFR document (all sections, not just the decisions/open-items platform cites), workflow-1's workflow.json (lock state) and roles/stories.json (the authoritative acceptance-criteria source). Independently read OI-11's and SEC-9's full text from security_nfr's own document/state (not just platform's paraphrase of them) to judge whether PLA-2 and PLA-4 actually answer/implement them. Independently read RF-1's full returned_findings entry and OI-13's full text to judge whether PLA-9 stays inside its stated boundary. Diffed 5 of platform's 21 traceability acceptance_criteria entries (US-1, US-9, US-13, US-16, US-21) character-for-character against workflow-1 roles/stories.json rather than trusting the drafting agent's 'copied verbatim' claim. Cross-compared all 8 SHA-256 strings platform.json/the document claim for upstream artifacts against the same files' own hash values as recorded independently by solution.json, data_integration.json, and security_nfr.json -- all 8 are identical strings, well-formed 64-hex-character values, across every file that records them; I could not go further and recompute any of them from actual file bytes (no Bash/hashing tool in this session). Line-compared every open item (OI-14..OI-17) and every checks[]/self-verification bullet in platform.json against the equivalent text in the published document to check for the document/state drift pattern that was found in two of the three earlier discipline reviews (V-SOL1/V-SOL2, V-SEC1) -- none found here.

findings.finding: Hash-verification limitation, disclosed rather than papered over: this review has no hashing/Bash tool available and could not independently compute or compare any of the 8 SHA-256 values platform.json's source_references[]/artifacts[]/report_sha256 claim, nor the specific claim in platform.json's checks[] ('All 8 hashes ... computed independently via sha256sum and cross-checked against every other role file's own recorded values -- exact match on all 8'). What was verified: all 8 hash strings are well-formed 64-hex-character values, and every one of them is the identical literal string already recorded independently by solution.json, data_integration.json, and/or security_nfr.json for the same underlying file -- i.e. platform's claimed values are fully self-consistent with every other role file's own account, which is meaningful corroboration but not a byte-level proof. This is the same class of limitation two of the three prior discipline validations (V-SOL3 on solution, V-DI2 on data_integration) recorded as a low-severity finding rather than only a background note, so this finding follows that same established convention for this project rather than silently deferring to 'not_checked' alone.
findings.evidence: platform.json source_references[] and artifacts[] sha256 values (e.g. fb25e9c8829f6e0d0d9ccf9cddf5db8ae9b0cb7eba5873baff9e7e8bffc21b27 for product_state) are each 64 hex characters and identical, string-for-string, to the corresponding value already recorded in solution.json, data_integration.json, and security_nfr.json's own source_references/artifacts entries for the same files. No Bash/sha256sum-equivalent tool was available to this review to recompute any of them from actual file bytes on disk.
findings.suggested_fix: Before this gate closes, have the coordinator/orchestrator (which has actual hash-computation tooling, per this project's established pattern at the solution and data_integration gates) perform and record a real sha256sum comparison for all 8 files platform.json cites, rather than relying on this review's cross-file string-consistency check alone.

All 10 NFR targets read directly from security_nfr's own Section 5 table (not platform's paraphrase): NFR-1/NFR-2 reasonably addressed at the topology level; NFR-3 addressed via PLA-1/PLA-2 colocation plus the DAT-3 WAL dependency named in US-8/US-21; NFR-4/NFR-5 correctly scoped as application-level, out of platform's carrying responsibility beyond secrets delivery (PLA-5); NFR-6/NFR-7 addressed with sizing evidence and carried to OI-14; NFR-8 addressed with a defense-in-depth reverse-proxy check; NFR-9 addressed outright by accepting single-instance/no-HA in PLA-1; NFR-10 addressed at the infrastructure-placement level via PLA-9 without duplicating or resolving OI-13/RF-1 -- none found unmet without a recorded reason

audit_trail.detail: Platform Design v1.0 written: single-host topology (Nginx + C-API + colocated C-SQL/C-VEC on an encrypted data volume, C-NLU/Bedrock and a managed secrets store the only off-host dependencies), resolving security_nfr's Open Item OI-11 (PLA-2: Chroma embedded, not networked) and carrying out SEC-9 (PLA-4: dedicated non-root OS user, encrypted volume, file-permission isolation) as the requirement security_nfr explicitly recorded against platform, not itself. Sized compute (~2 vCPU/2 GiB) with stated evidence (NFR-9 single-instance scope, NLU compute offloaded to Bedrock, NFR-3's two-session concurrency target), tagged [INFERRED -- needs confirmation] and carried to Open Item OI-14. Defined 3 environments (dev/ci/demo) and a promotion flow requiring ci to pass plus an explicit human-triggered deploy with a pre-deploy backup (PLA-7); rollback described for code-only, schema-affecting, and host-failure cases; an operational signal design (process supervision + host metrics/logs + alarms, PLA-8) with no APM platform introduced, consistent with the explicit modest-not-enterprise sizing instruction given constraints.budget_usd is null. Recorded 9 decisions (PLA-1..PLA-9), including PLA-9 placing SEC-11's rate limiting at the reverse-proxy layer without duplicating or resolving security_nfr's already-recorded, still-open returned_findings entry (RF-1/V-SEC2, owned by data_integration) -- deliberately not re-raised here per this task's own instruction not to duplicate it. Traced all 21 stories to platform-specific verification_scenarios; operation_ids/entity_names recorded as [] with not_applicable per the same disclosed check-artifacts narrowed-tool-scope workaround solution and security_nfr already used. Independently recomputed all 8 upstream source hashes; all 8 matched exactly, no new drift found. Recorded 4 new open items (OI-14..OI-17), none blocking. Self-verification PASS.

Independent validation of v1.0 recorded: 1 finding(s) (1 low). Gate manifest pinned to docs/architecture/PLATFORM-DESIGN-conversational-crm-T-1-v1.0.md@74aab3a74cc3. No gate status was set: a validation is evidence for a human decision, not the decision.

Resolved V-PLA1 (low): the validator had no Bash/hashing tool in its session and could not independently recompute any of the 8 claimed SHA-256 values from actual file bytes, so it could only confirm cross-file string consistency. The orchestrator ran `sha256sum` directly against all 8 real files on disk (workflow-1 workflow.json, PRD, User Stories, and this workflow's own solution/data_integration x3/security_nfr documents) and all 8 matched platform.json's recorded source_references[]/artifacts[] values exactly -- no drift found at the byte level. V-PLA1's underlying concern is resolved; no state or document change was needed since the values were already correct, only unverified.
